article.title: Recurrent IVF Failure isn’t the End of Journey; Personalised Treatment is Improving Success Rates: Fertility Experts - IndiaMedToday
article.summary: Recurrent IVF Failure isn’t the End of Journey; Personalised Treatment is Improving Success Rates: Fertility Experts IndiaMedTodayWorld IVF Day: Doctor Explains Potential Risks And Complications Couples Must Prepare To Manage NDTVEight IVF failures, then a miracle: Why IVF setbacks do not mean the end of parenthood The Indian ExpressAI rewrites fertility playbook, from embryo selection to sperm screening The Times of IndiaWorld IVF Day 2026: Why your 20s and 30s should include a reproductive health check-up Firstpost
article.full_text: The future of fertility treatment lies in precision medicine. Artificial intelligence is beginning to assist embryologists in selecting embryos with greater accuracy One unsuccessful IVF cycle does not mean the end of the road to parenthood. However, repeated IVF failures should not be overlooked or addressed by simply repeating the same treatment protocol, said leading fertility specialists from Radhakrishna Multispeciality Hospital & IVF Centre, Bengaluru, ahead of World IVF Day. Drawing on more than 35 years of experience in reproductive medicine, Dr. Vidya V. Bhat, Medical Director, Radhakrishna Multispeciality Hospital & IVF Centre, said that while IVF has transformed the lives of millions of couples across the world, it continues to be surrounded by myths, unrealistic expectations and social stigma. One of the most common misconceptions, she noted, is that IVF guarantees pregnancy. “IVF is among the most effective fertility treatments available today, but it is not a guarantee of success. Every embryo does not implant, and every IVF cycle provides valuable clinical insights. Rather than viewing a failed cycle as the end of the journey, we should understand why it happened and use that knowledge to improve the chances of success in future attempts,” she said. Dr. Vidya V. Bhat explained that recurrent IVF failure should trigger a thorough medical evaluation rather than an immediate repeat cycle. Current clinical practice recommends detailed investigations after two or more unsuccessful transfers of good-quality embryos, enabling specialists to identify underlying factors that may have gone undetected earlier. “Fertility science has advanced significantly over the past decade. We now know that successful implantation depends not only on the quality of the embryo but also on the health of the uterus, hormonal balance, sperm quality, genetics, lifestyle and several other factors. Every couple’s fertility journey is unique, and treatment should be equally personalised,” she said. Dr. Vidya V. Bhat highlighted that while embryo quality, particularly with advancing maternal age, remains one of the most important factors for IVF success, several other conditions can reduce the chances of implantation. These include uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, chronic endometrial inflammation, endometriosis, thyroid disorders, uncontrolled diabetes and hormonal imbalances. Dr. Vidya V. Bhat said that male fertility is often underestimated. “A routine semen analysis may appear normal, yet underlying sperm DNA damage can affect embryo development and pregnancy outcomes. Fertility is never a woman’s responsibility alone. Both partners must undergo a comprehensive evaluation to maximise the chances of success,” she said. Lifestyle, she said, plays a much larger role than many couples realise. Maintaining a healthy body weight, eating a balanced diet, exercising regularly, getting adequate sleep and avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol can significantly improve both egg and sperm quality. “While we cannot change age, there are many factors that couples can optimise before beginning another IVF cycle. Good reproductive health starts well before embryo transfer. Even modest lifestyle changes, combined with the right medical treatment, can make a meaningful difference,” she said. Speaking about recent advances in reproductive medicine, Dr. Vidya V. Bhat said IVF has become increasingly personalised. Sophisticated embryo culture systems, improved embryo selection techniques, selective genetic testing and advanced imaging technologies are helping fertility specialists better understand why implantation sometimes fails. “The future of fertility treatment lies in precision medicine. Artificial intelligence is beginning to assist embryologists in selecting embryos with greater accuracy, while ongoing research is deepening our understanding of the complex interaction between the embryo and the uterus during implantation,” she said. Dr. Vibha Bhat, Consultant Gynaecologist and Infertility specialist, Radhakrishna Multispeciality Hospital & IVF Centre. advised couples against rushing into another IVF cycle immediately after an unsuccessful attempt. “A brief pause can often be beneficial. It allows us to review previous treatment, reassess embryo quality, evaluate uterine health, investigate hormonal and metabolic disorders, and examine sperm quality more closely. Repeating the same treatment without understanding the cause of failure may simply lead to the same outcome,” she said. On the occasion of World IVF Day, Dr. Vidya V. Bhat encouraged couples facing recurrent IVF failure not to lose hope. “Over the past 35 years, I have seen many couples who believed parenthood was beyond their reach eventually welcome healthy babies. Recurrent IVF failure is not the end of the journey. In fact, it is often the point where we ask better questions, make more informed decisions and find better solutions. With today’s advances in reproductive medicine and a personalised approach to care, there is every reason to remain hopeful.”

story.title: The Third Signature
story.skipLabel: Recurrent IVF failure and personalised treatment

creativeDirection.dramaticPremise: After two unsuccessful embryo transfers, a woman reaches for the consent pen to repeat the same IVF plan immediately, then stops when the medical reality forces her to choose investigation and personalisation over panic.

dramaticSpine.characterGoal: Sign up today for another IVF cycle before fear and family pressure make her change her mind.
dramaticSpine.obstacle: She has already had two unsuccessful transfers and does not know whether repeating the same protocol will address the real cause.
dramaticSpine.newsCatalyst: Fertility specialists advise detailed evaluation after two or more unsuccessful transfers of good-quality embryos, and say personalised treatment can examine uterine health, hormones, sperm quality, genetics, lifestyle and other factors; AI is beginning to assist embryo selection.
dramaticSpine.reversal: With the pen poised, she realises another immediate repeat could simply reproduce the same approach without understanding why implantation failed.
dramaticSpine.costOfFailure: She may spend more emotionally and physically on another cycle without first addressing factors that could have gone undetected.
dramaticSpine.emotionalTurn: Her shame and urgency give way to a small, practical sense of control: asking better questions instead of treating failure as a verdict.
dramaticSpine.resolution: She leaves the consent line unsigned, records a request for a thorough review, and commits to a brief pause before deciding on another cycle.

visualBible.setting: A quiet animated fertility clinic consultation room just after closing, with one empty chair, a frosted glass door, a small desk, a consent form, a capped pen, and a phone showing an unanswered family call without readable text.
visualBible.colorAndLighting: Soft midnight-blue shadows outside the frosted door, warm amber desk lamp on the character, gentle rose highlights during her emotional turn; intimate, respectful, never clinical or cold.
recurringProps: cream appointment folder with blank pages
small ceramic cup of untouched tea
visualBible.storyArc: The room begins cramped and airless around an immediate signature; the space gradually opens through the window reflection as she chooses investigation and a pause rather than a reflexive repeat.

cast.role: fictional woman deciding whether to repeat IVF treatment
cast.voiceProfile: Intimate Indian-English voice with a low, slightly breathless texture; begins fast and tightly controlled, carrying embarrassment and urgency, uses clipped self-interruptions and one dry private joke, then slows into steadier warmth and cautious relief by the ending; perform as a private voice memo rather than a presentation, with earned pauses before difficult words.
cast.visualIdentity: Indian woman in her early thirties, shoulder-length wavy black hair, mustard cardigan over a pale blue kurta, small silver studs, canvas tote, expressive tired eyes; consistent wardrobe and appearance throughout.

beats.dramaticAction: Meera uncaps the consent pen, places its tip on the signature line, and starts recording a voice memo to her absent partner.
beats.turningPoint: Naming the news while reaching for the signature exposes the contradiction: she is about to repeat treatment before understanding what happened.

visual.caption: Recurrent IVF failure isn’t the end of the journey; personalised treatment is changing what comes next.
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film close-up of Meera uncapping a black pen over a blank consent form in a quiet fertility clinic room, her phone recording beside an untouched tea cup, warm desk lamp against midnight-blue shadows, low three-quarter camera, tense intimate mood, recurring mustard cardigan and pale blue kurta, clean caption-safe upper-third space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: The continuous scene opens on the pen hovering above the form as Meera records a private message in the empty consultation room.
visual.continuityNotes: Establish Meera, the desk, folder, phone, tea, lamp, and frosted door; preserve all props and wardrobe for the next shot.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Recurrent IVF failure isn’t the end of the journey—personalised treatment is changing what I do next. And I am saying that with this pen literally touching the line.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Two transfers. Two quiet goodbyes. I was going to sign for the same plan again before I could feel anything.

beats.dramaticAction: Her phone vibrates with an unanswered family call; Meera flips it face down, then pulls the folder toward herself instead of signing.
beats.turningPoint: She rejects the pressure to perform certainty and gives herself one moment to inspect the decision.

visual.caption: The fastest choice is not always the most informed one.
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film medium shot of Meera abruptly turning a vibrating phone face down and dragging a cream folder away from the signature line, empty chair behind her, warm lamp cutting through blue clinic shadows, handheld-feel camera angle, anxious restrained mood, recurring wardrobe and props, caption-safe upper-third space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: The phone tremor breaks the silence; Meera almost signs, then physically pulls the paperwork back and silences the call.
visual.continuityNotes: Continue directly from the pen close-up; the pen remains in her right hand, folder shifts toward her, phone is now face down.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: No. I cannot turn my panic into a signature just because somebody wants a neat answer tonight.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: A failed cycle gives clinical insights. Fine. Then I am not wasting mine by pretending it gave me nothing.

beats.dramaticAction: Meera opens the folder, circles the blank space for follow-up questions with the pen, and dictates them into her phone without calling anyone.
beats.turningPoint: The next cycle stops being an automatic repeat; it becomes conditional on a thorough review after two unsuccessful transfers.

visual.caption: After two or more unsuccessful transfers of good-quality embryos, specialists recommend detailed investigation before rushing into another cycle.
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film over-the-shoulder shot of Meera circling blank question spaces in a clinic folder while dictating into her phone, no readable writing, desk lamp illuminating her hands, frosted door and empty chair in background, thoughtful cinematic camera, focused but vulnerable mood, mustard cardigan and pale blue kurta visible, caption-safe upper-third space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: Meera turns the folder pages, refuses the signature, and builds a spoken list of questions in the same room.
visual.continuityNotes: Phone remains face down only until she lifts it to record; keep the pen, folder, tea, and lighting consistent. No readable document text appears.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: After two unsuccessful transfers, the next move is a proper investigation—not a photocopy of the last attempt.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Uterus. Hormones. Sperm quality. Genetics. Lifestyle. The embryo matters, yes—but apparently it is not travelling alone.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: And AI is beginning to help embryologists select embryos more accurately. Beginning. Not magic. I like that honesty.

beats.dramaticAction: Meera reaches for the pen again, writes nothing, and instead records a message requesting a review of the previous treatment, uterine health, hormonal and metabolic factors, and sperm quality.
beats.turningPoint: The same pen that would have committed her to repetition becomes a tool for postponing the cycle and demanding a personalised plan.

visual.caption: A brief pause can make room to review the previous treatment instead of repeating it blindly.
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film side profile of Meera holding the pen above a completely blank signature line while recording a firm voice memo, her reflection opening into the dark window, warm amber light on her face, deep blue room, intimate cinematic profile camera, cautious determination, recurring phone folder tea and wardrobe, caption-safe upper-third space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: Meera leans toward the desk as if to sign, stops, and turns the pen into a pointer for her own spoken request without writing on the form.
visual.continuityNotes: The folder stays open from the previous shot; preserve the blank signature area and face-down tea. Advance only her posture and emotional steadiness.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: I want the review first. What was checked, what was missed, and what changes before another transfer?

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Both partners. Not just me carrying the blame like it came free with the appointment.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Healthy weight, food, movement, sleep, no smoking, careful with alcohol—small changes, not a punishment parade.

beats.dramaticAction: Meera caps the pen, closes the unsigned folder, turns her phone screen-up, and walks toward the frosted door before stopping to send the recorded request.
beats.turningPoint: She gives up the immediate certainty of another cycle but leaves with an active plan: pause, review, and decide with personalised information.

visual.caption: She does not give up; she changes the next move.
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film wide shot of Meera standing from the desk, capping the pen and closing the unsigned folder, phone lifted as she sends a voice message near the frosted clinic door, warm light spilling behind her into blue hallway shadows, gentle low-angle camera, relieved but unresolved mood, mustard cardigan and pale blue kurta, tote at her side, caption-safe upper-third space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: The continuous scene ends as Meera sends the message, pockets the phone, and chooses the door instead of the signature.
visual.continuityNotes: Keep the folder unsigned and tucked under her arm; the pen is capped, tea remains untouched, and the same lamp glows behind her as she exits.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: I am taking the pause. Not because the journey is over—because repeating the same thing without answers is not bravery.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: I will ask better questions, get the review, and decide after that.

lines.speaker: meera
lines.text: Right now, the only thing I am signing is this message: do not rush me.

story.exit: Meera leaves the clinic with the unsigned folder under her arm, having chosen a personalised review and a brief pause before any further IVF cycle.
